summary: Specifies the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol, used between a Path Computation Client and a PCE or between PCEs. It carries path computation requests and replies and notifications for MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering, and is designed to be extensible. This is a Proposed Standard, extended by many later RFCs.

eli5.summary: One computer asks an expert computer, find me a good route for this traffic, and the expert replies. PCEP is the language for those questions and answers.

questions: how does a pce talk to a pcc
what is a path computation element
how does a pcc talk to a pce
subtitle: The protocol a router uses to ask a dedicated path computation server for a route, and to hear back.

tldr.problem: In the Path Computation Element model, the component that needs a traffic engineering path (the client) and the component that computes it (the PCE) can be separate. They need a common language, and the same one must work between a client and a PCE and between PCEs.
tldr.mechanism: PCEP runs over TCP. After an Open and Keepalive exchange, the client sends path computation requests (PCReq) made of typed objects, and the PCE answers with computed paths or a no-path reply (PCRep). Notification, error and close messages cover the rest.
tldr.outcome: PCEP is the base protocol, designed to be extended with new messages and objects. RFC 5440 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7896, RFC 8253, RFC 8356, RFC 9488 and RFC 9756.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: 7 (Open, Keepalive, PCReq, PCRep, PCNtf, PCErr, Close)

today: RFC 5440 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 7896, RFC 8253, RFC 8356, RFC 9488 and RFC 9756, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why PCEP Exists
sections.content:
RFC 4655 describes a model for computing paths for MPLS and GMPLS Traffic Engineering label switched paths (TE LSPs) in which the Path Computation Element (PCE) is separate from the Path Computation Client (PCC), and PCEs can cooperate. That needs a communication protocol, and RFC 4657 states the generic requirements: the same protocol must be used between a PCC and a PCE and between PCEs, and it must be easily extensible.

RFC 5440 specifies that protocol, the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). When describing PCE-to-PCE communication, the requesting PCE plays the role of a PCC. The RFC deliberately stays out of some questions: it assumes the PCE already has the topology and resource information it needs, and it says nothing about how a PCC discovers or selects a PCE, or how a path is calculated.
sections.eli5: Some routers ask a smart helper to work out the best route. PCEP is the set of words they use to ask and to answer.

sections.title: How PCEP Fits Together
sections.content:
PCEP operates over TCP, which provides reliable messaging and flow control, using the registered port 4189. A PCC may have sessions with several PCEs, and a PCE with many PCCs, but only one PCEP session and one TCP connection on the PCEP port can exist between a pair of peers at a time. Each message is a single transmission unit and parts of messages MUST NOT be interleaved.

Seven messages exist: Open and Keepalive set up and maintain a session, PCReq asks for a computation, PCRep answers it, PCNtf notifies of an event, PCErr reports errors, and Close ends a session.

A session can be kept open for an unlimited time, which suits frequent requests because it avoids opening a TCP connection each time. Alternatively it can be opened and closed for each request when requests are rare.
sections.eli5: There are seven kinds of messages, like hello, still-here, please-find-a-route, here-is-the-route, heads-up, oops and goodbye.

sections.title: Starting, Keeping and Ending a Session
sections.content:
Once TCP is up, each side's first message MUST be an Open, carrying session parameters such as the Keepalive timer and the DeadTimer. If the peer finds a parameter unacceptable it sends an error, and it SHOULD propose acceptable values in the OPEN object it returns. If a second Open still has unacceptable parameters, the receiver MUST send an error and immediately close the TCP connection. Acceptable parameters are acknowledged with a Keepalive, and the session is established once both peers have received one. The OpenWait and KeepWait timers are fixed at 1 minute.

Liveness uses two timers. A Keepalive timer restarts whenever a message is sent and, when it expires, a Keepalive is sent. A DeadTimer restarts whenever any message is received, and if it expires the session is declared dead. Any PCEP message counts as a keepalive. The minimum Keepalive is 1 second, the recommended value is 30 seconds, and the DeadTimer is recommended to be 4 times the peer's Keepalive. Setting the Keepalive to 0 turns the keepalives off, and the two sides may use different values.

To end a session a peer sends Close and then closes TCP. On receiving a valid Close, the other side MUST cancel all pending requests and close the connection. A TCP failure ends the session immediately.
sections.eli5: Both sides say hello and agree on how often to check in. If one goes quiet for too long, the other decides the call has dropped.

sections.title: Requests, Replies and Notifications
sections.content:
A PCReq must contain two objects, RP and END-POINTS, plus optional ones describing constraints such as bandwidth, metrics, an include route, LSP attributes and load balancing. Each request is identified by a Request-ID-number combined with the PCC and PCE addresses, and several can be outstanding at once. A PCReq may carry more than one request, and the PCE may process them in any order.

A PCRep must include an RP object with the matching Request-ID-number for each reply. On success it carries the computed paths as Explicit Route Objects (EROs). On failure it MUST include a NO-PATH object, which can say whether no path met the constraints or the PCE chain was broken, and can list the constraints that failed. For example, a PCE can echo the BANDWIDTH object or suggest a bandwidth for which a path could have been found.

Requests can be tied together with the SVEC object, which asks the PCE to compute a set of requests together and can demand that the paths share no link, no node or no SRLG. A LOAD-BALANCING object asks for a set of LSPs whose bandwidth adds up to a total, with a maximum count and a minimum bandwidth each.

PCNtf notifications let a PCC cancel pending requests, let a PCE cancel them, or let a PCE report that it is overloaded, optionally with an OVERLOADED-DURATION TLV. A PCC receiving an overload notice should consider backing off exponentially.
sections.eli5: You ask the helper for a route with some rules, like how wide the road must be. The helper hands back a route, or says no route fits and tells you which rule was the problem.

sections.title: The Common Header and Message Bodies
sections.content:
Every PCEP message begins with a common header holding a 3-bit Ver (version 1), 5 bits of flags (none defined), an 8-bit Message-Type and a 16-bit Message-Length giving the total length in bytes including the header. Types 1 to 7 are Open, Keepalive, Path Computation Request, Path Computation Reply, Notification, Error and Close.

The body is a set of objects, each either mandatory or optional, and the RFC defines the order allowed for each message with Backus-Naur Form. A message with a missing mandatory object MUST trigger an error. An unrecognized message gets a PCErr with Error-value 2 (capability not supported). If unknown messages arrive at a rate of MAX-UNKNOWN-MESSAGES per minute or more (recommended value 5), the receiver MUST send a Close and shut down the session.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a short label saying what it is and how long it is, followed by the details.

sections.title: Objects and TLVs
sections.content:
Objects share a common header: an 8-bit Object-Class, a 4-bit Object-Type, two reserved bits, a P flag, an I flag and a 16-bit Object Length. The length is always a multiple of 4. The P flag is set by a PCC to say the PCE must take the object into account. If a PCE does not understand or support such an object, it MUST reject the message with an error. The I flag lets a PCE say in a reply that it ignored an optional object.

Objects may contain TLVs: 2 bytes of type, 2 bytes of length, then the value, padded to 4-byte alignment. Unrecognized TLVs MUST be ignored. The defined objects include OPEN (class 1), RP (2), NO-PATH (3), END-POINTS (4, IPv4 or IPv6), BANDWIDTH (5, a 32-bit IEEE float in bytes per second), METRIC (6), ERO (7), RRO (8), LSPA (9), IRO (10), SVEC (11), NOTIFICATION (12), PCEP-ERROR (13), LOAD-BALANCING (14) and CLOSE.

The RP object carries a priority from 1 to 7, a reoptimization bit R, a bi-directional bit B, a strict/loose bit O and the 32-bit Request-ID-number. The METRIC object names a metric (IGP, TE or hop count) to optimize or bound, and the ERO and RRO reuse the encodings of the RSVP-TE objects of the same names. The LSPA object carries affinity masks and setup and holding priorities from 0 to 7.
sections.eli5: The details of a message are packed in labeled boxes, each with a tag saying what is inside and whether the helper really must follow it.

sections.title: Errors and Closing
sections.content:
A PCErr message MUST contain a PCEP-ERROR object with an Error-Type and an Error-value. If it answers a request, it includes the related RP objects. If the error happened during session setup, it does not. A single message may hold several error objects, and one PCErr is required per missing mandatory object.

Ten error types are defined: session establishment failure, capability not supported, unknown object, not supported object, policy violation, mandatory object missing, synchronized request missing, unknown request reference, attempt to establish a second session and invalid object. For a second session attempt, the existing session MUST be preserved and later messages about the second attempt silently ignored. Unknown request references or replies that arrive at MAX-UNKNOWN-REQUESTS per minute or more (recommended 5) force a Close.

The CLOSE object carries an optional reason: no explanation, DeadTimer expired, malformed message, too many unknown requests or replies, or too many unrecognized messages.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the helper sends a note saying exactly what the problem was. If too many confusing messages pile up, it hangs up the phone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats PCEP attacks as serious: forged or altered replies could lead a PCC to set up inappropriate LSPs, such as ones passing through parts of the network open to snooping or through congested links. Denial-of-service attacks could make a PCE too slow to be useful. The listed threats are spoofing, snooping, falsification and denial of service, and they matter most between ASes.

At the time of writing the only available TCP-level protection was TCP-MD5, and the RFC says implementations MUST support it, while noting its limitations and expecting the TCP Authentication Option to replace it. TLS is discussed as an alternative, but how PCEP would start TLS is left to future work. For privacy, TCP MAY run over IPsec tunnels, though the RFC worries that IPsec at that scale is hard to configure. Key management is discussed, including manual keys, a shared group key and key exchange protocols.

PCEs SHOULD be configurable with access policy, such as access lists of legitimate PCC addresses, and policy violations should be logged by lightweight mechanisms that cannot themselves be used for denial of service.
sections.eli5: If someone tricked the helper or listened in, they could send traffic down bad roads or learn your secret routes. So the two sides should prove who they are and keep the call private.

messages.label: Open
messages.note: The peer sends its own Open.

messages.label: PCReq
messages.note: RP and END-POINTS objects, plus optional constraints.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Starts session setup and proposes parameters.

items.label: Keepalive
items.desc: Keeps a session alive and acknowledges an Open.

items.label: Path Computation Request
items.desc: A PCC asks a PCE for a path.

items.label: Path Computation Reply
items.desc: A PCE returns paths or a no-path answer.

items.label: Notification
items.desc: Reports an event such as cancellation or overload.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: If set, the PCE must take the object into account.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: A PCE sets this to say it ignored an optional object.

fields.name: Object Length
fields.desc: Total object length in bytes; a multiple of 4.
